sections.html:
For most dwellings, one month's rent is the ceiling. General Obligations Law section 7-108(1-a) bars any deposit or advance above that amount, with carve-outs for seasonal units, owner-occupied co-op apartments and a few other housing types such as assisted living. Under the statute, the rule covers non-rent-stabilized units, and a lease can't waive it.

The tenant gets the whole deposit back at move-out, less reasonable, itemized charges for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, unpaid utilities owed to the landlord, and moving or storing belongings. A landlord can't charge for ordinary wear or for damage a previous tenant left.

  • Before move-in, the landlord must offer a walk-through, and if the tenant asks, both sign a written condition report.
  • Before move-out, the landlord must tell the tenant about the right to an inspection, held one to two weeks before the tenancy ends, on 48 hours' written notice.
  • Within 14 days after the tenant leaves, the landlord must send an itemized statement and the balance. Miss that deadline and the right to keep any part of the deposit is gone.
  • In a dispute the landlord has to prove the amount kept was reasonable, and a willful violation can bring punitive damages up to twice the deposit.

sections.h2: Who owes the deposit when a landlord sells?
sections.html:
The buyer can end up owing it. If the old landlord doesn't hand the deposit over, section 7-108(2) makes the new owner liable for the deposit plus interest whenever the buyer had actual knowledge of it. Knowledge is presumed in three situations.

When a buyer is treated as knowing about a tenant deposit
SituationWhat follows
Deposit placed in a bank in the six months before closingBuyer is deemed to know of it
Deposit acknowledged in a lease in effect at closingBuyer is deemed to know of it
Tenant supplies a cancelled check, receipt or signed lease from a prior ownerBuyer is deemed to know of it
No record of a deposit anywhereBuyer must send written notice within 30 days after closing, and the tenant has 30 days to show proof

A buyer who finds no record can demand that the seller set up an escrow account equal to one month's rent to cover a late claim. Sellers who keep clean deposit records and give the buyer copies at closing avoid that argument entirely.

sections.h2: Notice for rent increases and non-renewal
sections.html:
A rent increase of 5 percent or more, or a decision not to renew, requires written notice, and the length depends on how long the tenant has lived there. Real Property Law section 226-c sets 30 days for under one year of occupancy, 60 days for one to two years and 90 days for more than two years or a lease of at least two years. Whichever is longer, the tenant's total time in the home or the lease term, governs.

Late notice doesn't void the change. The tenancy simply continues on its existing terms from the day written notice arrives until the full notice period has run. Under the version in force until June 15, 2034, the notice must also say whether the unit falls under Article 6-A, the good cause eviction law, and if it is exempt, why.

Section 214 lists the exemptions. They include owner-occupied buildings with no more than ten units, small landlords who disclose their ownership, condominium and cooperative units, rent-regulated units and homes with a certificate of occupancy issued on or after January 1, 2009 for thirty years. Section 214 also refers to local laws adopted by villages, towns and cities outside New York City, so ask the local clerk whether yours has one.

Every residential lease, written or oral, carries an implied promise that the home and the common areas are fit to live in. Real Property Law section 235-b says occupants can't be subjected to conditions dangerous, hazardous or harmful to life, health or safety, and any waiver by the tenant is void.

  • A condition caused by the tenant, or by someone the tenant directs, is not a breach.
  • A court assessing damages doesn't need expert testimony.
  • For rent-regulated homes, damages are reduced by any rent reduction the state housing agency already ordered for the same problem.

The warranty applies to every residential lease in the building, so settle open repair complaints before you list.

sections.h2: Can a landlord evict without going to court?
sections.html:
No. Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law section 711 says no tenant or lawful occupant of a dwelling may be removed except in a special proceeding. The same section defines a squatter as a person who enters or stays on property without the owner's permission or any right, and says a squatter is not a tenant.

The usual grounds are a tenant staying after the lease ends and a tenant in default on rent. For unpaid rent, the landlord must serve a written demand giving at least 14 days to pay or leave, following the service rules in section 735. Until June 15, 2034, that notice also has to carry the Article 6-A disclosure described above.

Two smaller duties come up in nonpayment cases. Under section 235-e, a landlord who takes cash or any payment other than the tenant's personal check must give a written receipt showing the date, amount, premises, period covered, and signature and title. If rent isn't received within five days of the due date, the landlord must send a notice by certified mail, and skipping it is an affirmative defense for the tenant in a nonpayment case.

Often the tenant still owes part of the rent. Real Property Law section 227-e requires a landlord whose tenant leaves in breach of the lease to act in good faith and take reasonable, customary steps to re-rent at fair market value or the old rent, whichever is lower. When a new tenant's lease starts, it ends the earlier lease and reduces what the first tenant owes.

Whoever asks for damages carries the burden of proof, and a lease clause excusing the landlord from mitigating is void as against public policy. If you're also thinking of selling, keep records of advertising and showings, because that is the evidence a court will want.

sections.h2: Preparing to sell a New York rental
sections.html:
Begin with paperwork. Collect every lease, the deposit records and the dates of the last rent notices, because the buyer's attorney will ask for them and a buyer can be liable for any deposit it knew about. Check rent receipts too, since a gap in receipts can matter if a nonpayment case follows.

  • Confirm whether any unit is rent-regulated or exempt from the good cause law, and note the reason.
  • Don't try to remove a tenant yourself. A special proceeding in court is required.
  • Time any non-renewal or rent notice to the 30, 60 or 90 day schedule so it doesn't become an argument at closing.
  • Resolve habitability complaints in writing, since they carry over to the buyer.

Rent-regulated homes follow separate laws: the rent stabilization law, the city rent and rehabilitation law and the emergency housing rent control law. Ask your attorney which regime covers your building.

faqs.q: What is the maximum security deposit in New York?
faqs.a: One month's rent for most dwellings. The cap comes from General Obligations Law section 7-108(1-a), which lists exceptions such as seasonal units and owner-occupied co-op apartments.

faqs.q: How fast must a landlord return a deposit?
faqs.a: Within 14 days after the tenant has moved out, with an itemized statement of any deductions. A landlord who misses the deadline gives up the right to keep any part of it.

faqs.q: How much notice is needed for a New York rent increase?
faqs.a: For an increase of 5 percent or more, 30 days if the tenant has lived there under a year, 60 days for one to two years and 90 days beyond that, under Real Property Law section 226-c.

faqs.q: Can a buyer be held liable for a deposit the seller kept?
faqs.a: Yes, when the buyer had actual knowledge of it. Deposits in a bank within six months of closing or named in a lease then in force count as known to the buyer.

faqs.q: Who counts as a squatter in New York?
faqs.a: A person who enters or stays on property with no permission, title or right. Under RPAPL section 711, a squatter is not a tenant, though a lawful tenant can only be removed through a special proceeding.
